title: Anger, Annoyance & Animal Idioms
description: Express degrees of anger and understand everyday animal idioms.

source.title: Advanced Grammar & Vocabulary — Express Publishing
source.note: Lesson explanations, examples and practice have been adapted for independent study from the supplied unit. Answers and explanations are editorial, not a publisher answer key.

lessons.title: Degrees of anger
lessons.body: Annoyed and irritated often describe a mild reaction. Furious and livid express strong anger. Cross is common in everyday British English. Tone and context affect the strength of any word.
examples: I am irritated by the noise.
She was absolutely livid about the damage.

lessons.title: The person or the cause?
lessons.body: An irritated person feels annoyance. An irritating noise causes it. Furious describes a person’s reaction; galling describes something frustrating because it seems unfair.
examples: The delay was irritating; the passengers were irritated.
It was galling to lose after all that work.

lessons.title: Keep the whole expression
lessons.body: Idioms use fixed words and prepositions. Learn the expression as a chunk, including the verb. Their verb forms still change with tense.
examples: get on my nerves; drive me up the wall
She hit the roof; he blew his top.
They are up in arms about the proposal.

lessons.title: Animal words can become verbs
lessons.body: Dog, duck, hound, rabbit and worm can function as verbs in figurative or extended senses. Their tense must fit the sentence.
examples: She ducked to avoid the ball.
He wormed his way out of the task.

lessons.title: Use idioms with care
lessons.body: Animal idioms are usually informal and can be vivid or critical. Understand the meaning before using one about another person. A dark horse is little known; a wild goose chase is a futile search.
examples: The new candidate is a dark horse.
We had a whale of a time at the party.

vocabulary.example: The neighbours had a blazing row.
vocabulary.note: Row rhymes with cow in this meaning.

vocabulary.example: Dad blew his top over the bill.
The teacher looked cross.
I feel crotchety when I am tired.
That buzzing is driving me up the wall.
vocabulary.note: Informal; pronoun changes with the person.

vocabulary.example: She was furious about the mistake.
The unfair result was galling.
The repeated tapping gets on my nerves.

vocabulary.definition: An argument with strong feelings and anger.
vocabulary.example: They had a heated argument about money.
He hit the roof when he saw the damage.

vocabulary.definition: Angry at something thought unfair or insulting.
vocabulary.example: She was indignant at the accusation.
His dishonesty infuriates me.
Irate passengers demanded a refund.
The noise irritates her.
He was absolutely livid.
vocabulary.note: Normally after a linking verb in this sense.

vocabulary.definition: Unwilling to do something, often because of anger.
vocabulary.example: I am in no mood to argue.

vocabulary.definition: A sudden strong expression of emotion, often anger.
vocabulary.example: She regretted her angry outburst.

vocabulary.definition: A tendency to become angry easily.
vocabulary.example: He has a quick temper.
vocabulary.note: Not a fast temper in this collocation.

vocabulary.example: I am sick and tired of waiting.
vocabulary.note: Follow of with a noun or -ing form.

vocabulary.definition: Show uncontrolled anger, often by crying or shouting.
vocabulary.example: The child threw a tantrum.
He is touchy about his age.

vocabulary.definition: Very angry and ready to protest.
vocabulary.example: Residents are up in arms about the closure.

vocabulary.definition: A person regarded as different or a disappointment in a family.
vocabulary.example: He felt like the black sheep of the family.
Without my glasses, I am as blind as a bat.

vocabulary.definition: For a very long time, usually with little result.
vocabulary.example: You can argue till the cows come home.
vocabulary.note: Also until the cows come home.

vocabulary.definition: A person whose abilities or plans are little known.
vocabulary.example: The new entrant is a dark horse.
The project was dogged by delays.
We have been friends for donkey’s years.

vocabulary.definition: Lower your head or body to avoid something.
vocabulary.example: She ducked under the branch.

vocabulary.definition: Criticism or trouble that has no effect on someone.
vocabulary.example: The remarks were water off a duck’s back to him.
vocabulary.note: Usually like water off a duck’s back.

vocabulary.example: Something about the offer seems fishy.
Reporters hounded the actor.
She did the lion’s share of the work.

vocabulary.definition: Talk for too long in a boring way.
vocabulary.example: He rabbited on about his hobby.
Sorry I was ratty this morning.

vocabulary.term: have a whale of a time
vocabulary.example: We had a whale of a time.

vocabulary.definition: A search unlikely to achieve anything.
vocabulary.example: The false address sent us on a wild goose chase.

vocabulary.definition: Avoid a duty through clever excuses.
vocabulary.example: He wormed his way out of cleaning.
vocabulary.note: Follow of with a noun or -ing form.

exerciseGroups.title: Choose the expression
exerciseGroups.instruction: Choose the word or phrase that completes the sentence.

questions.prompt: I was absolutely ___ when they cancelled again.
questions.explanation: Absolutely commonly intensifies the strong adjective livid.

questions.prompt: He loses his temper easily: he has a ___ temper.
questions.explanation: The fixed collocation is quick temper.

questions.prompt: The most ___ thing is that he never apologised.
questions.explanation: Galling describes a frustrating or unfair situation.

questions.prompt: She is often a bit ___ in the morning.
questions.explanation: Crotchety means irritable or bad-tempered.

questions.prompt: The child threw a ___.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is throw a tantrum.

questions.prompt: Mum will hit the ___ when she sees the damage.
questions.explanation: Hit the roof means become very angry.

questions.prompt: That tapping gets on my ___.
questions.explanation: The expression is get on someone’s nerves.

questions.prompt: I am ___ to listen to these excuses.
questions.explanation: In no mood takes to + verb; sick and tired takes of.

questions.prompt: The drilling is driving me up the ___.
questions.explanation: Drive someone up the wall means annoy them intensely.

questions.prompt: Residents are up in ___ about the new tax.
questions.explanation: Up in arms describes angry protest.

questions.prompt: They had a ___ row in the restaurant.
questions.explanation: Blazing row is a fixed collocation for an angry argument.

exerciseGroups.title: Complete the animal idiom
exerciseGroups.instruction: Type the missing animal word or the appropriate form of it.

questions.prompt: His career was ___ by injuries.
questions.explanation: Dogged by means repeatedly troubled by.

questions.prompt: Double my money overnight? That sounds ___.
questions.explanation: Fishy means suspicious.

questions.prompt: Criticism is like water off a ___ back to her.
questions.explanation: The full phrase is water off a duck’s back.

questions.prompt: Without his glasses, he is as blind as a ___.
questions.explanation: The fixed comparison is as blind as a bat.

questions.prompt: We had a ___ of a time at the party.
questions.explanation: A whale of a time means a very enjoyable time.

questions.prompt: You can argue till the ___ come home.
questions.explanation: The expression means for a very long time.

questions.prompt: If I had not ___, the ball would have hit my head.
questions.explanation: Duck is a verb meaning lower your head or body.

questions.prompt: We know little about the new finalist: a dark ___.
questions.explanation: A dark horse is someone little known.

questions.prompt: Searching that false address was a wild ___.
questions.explanation: A wild goose chase is a futile search.

questions.prompt: She deserves the ___ share of the profits.
questions.explanation: The lion’s share is the largest part.

questions.prompt: He was treated as the black ___ of the family.
questions.explanation: Black sheep describes a family outsider or perceived disappointment.

questions.prompt: You cannot ___ your way out of the washing-up.
questions.explanation: Worm your way out of means evade a duty.

questions.prompt: He ___ on about the same topic for hours.
questions.explanation: Rabbit on means talk at excessive length.
